title: What is hCRI.io?
content:
hCRI.io is a free tool for analyzing the color rendering quality of light sources — flashlights, LED bulbs, grow lights, studio lights, and more. Upload a spectral power distribution (SPD) file from a spectrometer and get a full IES TM-30-18 color rendition report instantly.

No installation required. Works in any browser. Supports CSV files from popular instruments like the Hopoocolor HPCS-330, as well as JSON and CGATS formats.

For a closer look at the standard behind these numbers, see IES TM-30-18 Overview.

title: Getting Started
content:
Guest mode: Click "Analyze" (or paste data) to analyze a file without creating an account. Results are shown immediately but not saved.

Registered accounts: Create a free account to save reports, compare sources side-by-side, generate share links, and download PDF reports. Sign in with your email address or username.

Uploading: Drag a measurement file (CSV, TSV, TXT, JSON, SP or PDF; see What files can I upload?) onto the upload area, or click to browse. The instrument model and firmware version are automatically detected from the file header and shown in the report.

See Share Links and Share Card for more on sharing a report once it's saved.

title: What files can I upload?
content:
hCRI.io accepts:

• CSV — from instruments like the Hopoocolor HPCS-330 and HPCS-600. Wavelength and intensity columns are detected automatically.
• JSON — from open-source or DIY spectrometers in standard format.
• CGATS — the IES/CIE standard spectral data format.
• ZIP — a zip archive of any of the above. Each supported file inside is analyzed and saved as its own report; anything unsupported inside the zip is skipped.

You can select or drag more than one file at a time (including a mix of individual files and a zip). They're uploaded one after another, and you'll see a short progress note and a summary when it's done.

Files should cover approximately 380–780nm. The instrument model, firmware version, and all raw header fields are preserved and shown in the report's Raw Instrument Data panel.

Prefer scripting it? See Uploading via the API.

title: IES TM-30-18 Overview
content:
IES TM-30-18 is the current industry standard for evaluating color rendition of light sources, published by the Illuminating Engineering Society. It replaced the older CRI (Ra) system with two complementary metrics: Rf (Fidelity) and Rg (Gamut).

TM-30 uses 99 color evaluation samples (CES) spanning the full visible spectrum, compared to CRI's 8 samples, making it far more accurate and comprehensive. The standard also includes the Color Vector Graphic (CVG) and local hue-bin analysis.

See Rf — Color Fidelity Index and Rg — Color Gamut Index for details on each metric.

title: Rf — Color Fidelity Index
content:
Rf measures how accurately colors are rendered compared to a reference illuminant of the same color temperature. Scale is 0–100 where 100 is perfect fidelity.

• 90–100: Excellent. Colors appear nearly identical to reference. Ideal for art galleries, medical, photography.
• 80–89: Very Good. Minor differences only visible under close comparison. Suitable for retail, offices, high-quality residential.
• 70–79: Good. Noticeable shifts in saturated colors. Acceptable for general commercial use.
• Below 70: Low. Significant color distortion. Avoid for any color-sensitive application.

See Rg — Color Gamut Index for the companion gamut metric, and Local Color Fidelity (Rf,hj) for a hue-by-hue breakdown.

title: Rg — Color Gamut Index
content:
Rg measures the average size of the color gamut rendered by the light source compared to the reference. Scale is typically 60–140.

• Rg = 100: Same gamut as reference illuminant.
• Rg > 100: Colors appear more vivid/saturated than reference (gamut expansion). Often preferred in retail.
• Rg < 100: Colors appear less saturated/duller than reference (gamut compression).
• Rg 85–115 is generally considered the acceptable range for quality sources.

See Rf — Color Fidelity Index for the companion fidelity metric, and Color Vector Graphic (CVG) for a visual picture of gamut change by hue.

title: CCT — Correlated Color Temperature
content:
CCT describes the "warmth" or "coolness" of a light source, measured in Kelvin (K).

• 2700–3000K: Warm white. Cozy, residential feel.
• 3500–4000K: Neutral white. Clean and natural. Popular for offices and retail.
• 5000–6500K: Cool/daylight white. Crisp and energizing.

Note: CCT alone says nothing about color quality — a 3000K LED can have Rf 95 or Rf 60. That's why TM-30 matters.

See Duv — Distance from Planckian Locus for the companion tint measurement.

title: Duv — Distance from Planckian Locus
content:
Duv measures how far the light source's color point sits from the Planckian locus (the black body curve — the path of perfect thermal emitters).

• Duv near 0: On the black body curve. Neutral, natural appearance.
• Duv positive (+): Above the locus. Slight green/yellow tint.
• Duv negative (−): Below the locus. Slight pink/rosy tint.
• |Duv| < 0.006: Excellent. Within ANSI acceptable range.
• |Duv| 0.006–0.012: Noticeable but acceptable for many applications.
• |Duv| > 0.012: Clearly visible tint, may be objectionable.

See CCT — Correlated Color Temperature for the companion warmth measurement, and CIE 1931 Chromaticity Diagram to see Duv plotted visually.

title: Ra — CRI (Color Rendering Index)
content:
Ra is the original CRI metric from CIE 13.3-1995, still widely used in product specs and datasheets. It averages 8 moderately saturated color samples (R1–R8).

Limitations: CRI only tests 8 colors, has no strongly saturated red sample, and can be gamed by LED phosphors. TM-30's Rf is more accurate and comprehensive. Both are shown so you can compare against manufacturer specs.

See Rf — Color Fidelity Index for TM-30's more accurate alternative, and R9 — Red Saturation for a critical sample CRI leaves out of its average.

title: R9 — Red Saturation
content:
R9 is the 9th special CRI sample — a strongly saturated red. It is not included in the Ra average but is critically important for skin tones, meat display, red objects, and photography.

• R9 ≥ 50: Good red rendering.
• R9 ≥ 80: Excellent. Required for high-end photography and medical.
• R9 < 0: Poor red rendering. Reds will appear desaturated or distorted.

See CRI R1–R15 Bar Chart to see R9 alongside the other 14 samples, and Ra — CRI (Color Rendering Index) for the average it's excluded from.

title: CRI R1–R15 Bar Chart
content:
The bar chart on the report page shows the individual CIE 13.3 Color Rendering Index scores for all 15 test color samples, each from 0 to 100. A longer bar means the source renders that particular color more faithfully relative to a reference illuminant of the same CCT.

• R1–R8: moderately saturated pastel colors. Their average is Ra, the general CRI value quoted on most datasheets.
• R9: strong saturated red — the most demanding and most revealing sample (see R9 — Red Saturation).
• R10–R12: saturated yellow, green, and blue.
• R13: light (caucasian) skin tone.
• R14: leaf green / foliage.
• R15: a second, asian skin-tone sample.

When your instrument reports R-values directly in the file, those measured values are shown; otherwise hCRI computes each Ri from the uploaded spectrum. Hover or tap the “?” on the chart for a quick summary.

See CES — Color Evaluation Samples for TM-30's equivalent at full 99-sample resolution.

title: Metric Boxes — Customize Your Dashboard
content:
The metric boxes below the Color Vector Graphic (CVG) wheel are fully customizable:

• Drag to reorder — grab the ⠿ handle and drag any box to a new position.
• Remove — click the ✕ on any box to hide it.
• Add — click the + Add button to restore hidden metrics or add extra values from the raw instrument data (illuminance, S/P ratio, dominant wavelength, purity, and other numeric fields your instrument records). Reports with a full visible spectrum also offer an LER (lm/W) box; see LER — Luminous Efficacy of Radiation.
• Reset — open the Add menu and click Reset to restore the default layout.

Your layout is saved per-report in browser storage.

See Color Vector Graphic (CVG) for the chart these boxes sit alongside.

title: Color Vector Graphic (CVG)
content:
The CVG is TM-30's visual representation of how a light source renders the 16 hue-angle bins across the full color circle. The red polygon shows the test source; the black circle is the reference.

• Points outside the circle: That hue range is rendered more saturated (chroma increase).
• Points inside the circle: That hue range is rendered less saturated (chroma decrease).
• Rotation of points: Indicates a hue shift in that color region.

The 16 numbered positions correspond to hue-angle bins starting at red (1) and proceeding around the color wheel.

On the report this graphic sits in a row with the CRI R1–R15 Bar Chart and the CIE 1931 Chromaticity Diagram, stacking on narrow screens. Each chart has a “?” button that explains it.

title: Local Color Fidelity (Rf,hj)
content:
The bar chart shows Rf broken down into the same 16 hue-angle bins as the CVG. This tells you which specific color ranges are rendered well vs poorly.

For example, a source might have Rf 88 overall but show Rf 65 in the cyan-green range (bins 7–9), which would affect how it renders teal fabrics or plant foliage.

See Rf — Color Fidelity Index for the single overall score this chart breaks down by hue.

title: SPD — Spectral Power Distribution
content:
The SPD chart shows how much power the light source emits at each wavelength across the measured range (commonly ~380–780nm, but the axis spans whatever range your file provides). The colored bars show the test source; the dashed grey line shows the reference blackbody/daylight illuminant at the same CCT.

• 380–440nm: Violet
• 440–490nm: Blue
• 490–560nm: Green
• 560–590nm: Yellow
• 590–625nm: Orange
• 625–780nm: Red

Smooth, broad spectra generally render colors better than narrow peaked spectra.

See Calculation Methods & Sources for how the spectrum is interpolated and compared to the reference illuminant.

title: LER — Luminous Efficacy of Radiation
content:
LER says how many lumens of visible light a source makes for each watt of optical (radiated) power. It is a property of the spectrum alone, so it ignores electrical efficiency: a spectrum with more power near 555 nm (green-yellow, where the eye is most sensitive) scores higher than one with the same power in deep red or violet.

HOW IT'S CALCULATED
LER = 683.002 × ∫ V(λ)·S(λ) dλ ÷ ∫ S(λ) dλ, over 380–780 nm, where S is your spectrum and V(λ) is the CIE photopic sensitivity curve. Examples: a flat spectrum is about 182 lm/W, a 555 nm line is 683 lm/W, and a 5800 K blackbody over 400–700 nm is about 251 lm/W.

THE RANGE
Only the part of 380–780 nm your instrument actually measured is used; nothing is guessed outside it. If the measurement stops short of 380 or 780 nm by more than 5 nm the value is marked with * (partial), because the missing ends make it a little different from a full-range LER.

WHERE YOU SEE IT
• An LER (lm/W) box among the metric boxes (hide, add and drag it like the others).
• An LER chart card next to the SPD, chroma, hue and fidelity charts, showing your spectrum, the eye's V(λ) curve over it, and the part the eye counts filled in. Drag the cards to reorder them.
• Toggles on the chart swap the V(λ) curve for the CIE S 026 alpha-opic curves (S, M and L cones, rods, melanopic) to see how much of your spectrum each one counts. Hover a toggle for what it means. These curves are for comparison only; LER itself always uses V(λ).

See SPD — Spectral Power Distribution for the chart it builds on, and Calculation Methods & Sources for the standards.

title: CES — Color Evaluation Samples
content:
The bottom bar shows Rf for each of TM-30's 99 Color Evaluation Samples, arranged by hue angle. Each bar represents one color sample colored to represent its approximate hue. Taller bars mean higher fidelity for that color. This gives the most detailed view of where a light source succeeds and struggles.

See CRI R1–R15 Bar Chart for CRI's equivalent at a coarser 15-sample resolution, and IES TM-30-18 Overview for how these samples are used.

title: CIE 1931 Chromaticity Diagram
content:
The CIE 1931 xy chromaticity diagram now appears directly on the report page, in a row with the Color Vector Graphic and the CRI R1–R15 bars (the charts stack on narrow screens). It maps any color to two coordinates, x and y.

• The horseshoe-shaped outline (the spectral locus) encloses every color the human eye can see; pure single-wavelength colors lie along its curved edge.
• The curve inside it is the Planckian (blackbody) locus — the path an ideal incandescent radiator follows as its temperature rises. Points along it are the neutral “white” points for each CCT.
• Isotherm lines crossing the locus indicate correlated color temperature (CCT).
• Your source is plotted as a single point at its (x, y). How far that point sits above or below the Planckian locus is the Duv value.

A point on the locus reads as neutral white; the further off it, the more tinted (greenish above, pink/magenta below). The previous CIE 1960 (uv), CIE 1976 (u'v') and SDCM diagrams have been removed to keep the report focused on the most widely used view.

See Duv — Distance from Planckian Locus and CCT — Correlated Color Temperature for what this diagram's locus and isotherms represent.

title: Share Links
content:
Each saved report can be shared via a public link. Click "🔗 Share Link" in the report header to generate a URL anyone can open without logging in.

The full TM-30 report is visible to anyone with the link, including the instrument model, SPD, CVG, all chromaticity diagrams, and raw instrument data.

You can revoke a share link at any time — the old URL stops working immediately. Revoking one report's link does not affect other reports.

See Share Card for a downloadable image alternative.

title: Share Card
content:
The "↗ Share Card" button generates a portrait image summarizing the key metrics: Rf, Rg, CCT, Duv, Ra, R9, the SPD chart (with reference blackbody line), CVG wheel, and Rf,hj bin chart. Download as PNG to share on forums, social media, or include in a review.

See Share Links for a full interactive alternative to this static image.

title: Raw Data Download
content:
Raw data download is OFF by default. When it is on for a report, that report's page shows a Raw Instrument Data section: the instrument's header fields and the full wavelength table, with a button to download them as a CSV. Only signed-in users see it, including on public reports in Explore. It is never offered to logged-out visitors or on share-link pages.

PER REPORT
Open one of your reports and tick Allow raw data download (next to Exclude Report From Explore). Untick it to turn it off again; the section disappears for everyone right away.

YOUR DEFAULT
Profile → Privacy → "Allow raw data download on my new reports" sets the starting value for reports you upload from now on (including uploads from the Companion app and the API). It never changes reports you already have on its own. To change them all at once, press the button under it ("Turn on / Turn off for all my existing reports"), which applies your current default to every report you own after a confirmation. Each report can then be switched individually.

WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE TURNING IT ON
A downloadable spectrum is easy to copy in bulk. Automated scrapers and other sites can collect, republish or reuse your measurements, and turning the switch off later cannot take back copies already made. Leave it off unless you want the data to be reusable.

The license you choose appears at the top of the CSV (see Report Licenses). See Profile & Account Settings for the Privacy tab and Share Links for sharing a report.

title: Report Licenses
content:
A license tells people what they may do with your report and its data. It is a statement of your wishes; it does not stop anyone from copying what they can see, so use it together with Raw Data Download if you want control over the data itself.

CHOOSING ONE
• On a report: use the License menu on your own report page (next to Allow raw data download).
• As your default: Profile → Privacy → License for my reports sets the starting license for reports you upload from now on. Existing reports keep theirs unless you press Apply to all my existing reports, which sets every report you own to your default license (after a confirmation).
• Admins can set it from the admin report editor.
If you choose nothing, the report is "All rights reserved".

THE CHOICES
• All rights reserved — people may look but need your permission to reuse it.
• CC0 — you give up your rights; anyone may use it for anything, with no credit needed.
• CC BY — anyone may reuse it, even commercially, if they credit you.
• CC BY-SA — like CC BY, but anything built from it must use the same license.
• CC BY-NC — reuse with credit, but not for commercial purposes.
• CC BY-ND — reuse with credit, but only unchanged.
• CC BY-NC-SA — credit, non-commercial, and share alike.
• CC BY-NC-ND — credit, non-commercial, and no changes.
The Creative Commons versions are version 4.0. Each one links to the official summary and full text at creativecommons.org; the overview page is https://creativecommons.org/share-your-work/cclicenses/

WHERE IT SHOWS
It appears on the report page for everyone who views it (including share links and Explore), at the top of any raw data CSV download, and as "license" in the API. Once someone has used your data under a license, changing the license later does not undo that.

This is general information, not legal advice. See Raw Data Download for who can download your data.

title: Profile & Account Settings
content:
Click your name in the sidebar to open your profile. From there you can:

• Change your password — enter current and new password directly, or click "send a reset link to your email" to get a fresh link without needing your current password.
• Change your email — requires your current password to confirm.
• Change your display name — your name is also accepted as a login username.

You can log in with either your email address or your username (case-insensitive).

See Uploading via the API for the API tokens managed from this page.

title: Site Announcements
content:
Occasionally a banner appears at the top of the site (and sometimes on report pages) with news, a warning, or notice of maintenance. Each has an icon and a color for its type: information, news, success, warning, site issue, important or alert. It follows your light or dark theme.

Click × to dismiss a banner. Your browser remembers it with a cookie, so it stays away until the message is changed or replaced by a new one, or you clear your cookies. Some urgent messages have no ×.

FOR ADMINS
Admin → Notices creates and edits banners: type, icon, location (top, report page, or both), message, start and stop time (or a duration), enabled, and whether it can be dismissed. A live preview shows how it will look, and each entry is labeled live, scheduled, ended or disabled. Saving a banner resets everyone's dismissal so they see it again.

title: My Reports & Folders
content:
"My Reports" (in the Explore tab) is your personal library — every report you've uploaded, public or private.

Folders let you organize that library. Click "+ New Folder" at the top of My Reports to create one. A report can belong to at most one folder; folders live only inside My Reports and don't affect Explore.

Adding reports to a folder:
• Drag a report card onto a folder tile.
• Check the boxes on several report cards first — dragging any one of the checked cards moves the whole selection together.
• Or open a report and use the folder button (📁) next to "← Back to My Reports" to pick a folder, or create a new one on the spot, without leaving the report.

Opening a folder shows only what's inside it, with a report count and a "← Back to My Reports"/"← Back to [Folder Name]" link depending on where you are. Reports filed into a folder no longer appear in the main My Reports list — only inside that folder.

To remove a report from a folder, drag it onto the "Drag here to remove from folder" zone that appears while you're inside a folder (desktop only), or use the report's own 📁 button and choose "Remove from folder." Emptying a folder completely takes you back to My Reports automatically. Deleting a folder (from inside it) moves its reports back to the main list rather than deleting them.

See Filtering & Search, Comparing Reports, and Bulk Actions — Categorize & Delete for more on working with your library.

title: Comparing Reports
content:
Check the boxes on up to 12 report cards (in Explore, My Reports, or a folder) to select them for comparison. "Select all (up to 12)" grabs the reports currently on screen in one click, and "Clear" empties the selection — both sit right next to the report count.

Click "Compare →" to open the comparison view. The Cards tab lines the selected reports up side-by-side; the Overlay tab plots their spectral power distributions on one chart. Drag a card to reorder it.

Click any card in the comparison view to open that report full-size — you'll see the same guest preview a stranger would if you're not signed in, or the full report with your normal owner controls if you are (and if it's yours).

Use "↗ Share Card" from the comparison view to export a PNG image of the cards or overlay for sharing outside the site.

See My Reports & Folders for organizing reports before you compare them.

title: Filtering & Search
content:
The filters sidebar (search, category dropdowns, and range sliders for CCT, Duv, Ra, Rf, Rg, and R9) narrows down whatever list you're currently looking at.

On My Reports and inside folders, filters start out inactive — you're shown everything until you touch one. The moment you adjust a slider, pick a category, or type a search term, filtering switches on for that view. "Reset Filters" turns it back off and clears everything you'd set. On Explore, filters are always active.

Category dropdowns (Light Brand, Light Model, LED CCT, LED Brand, LED Model, Optic) have a search box at the top — type a few letters to jump to a value in a long list instead of scrolling.

A report with more than one LED matches an LED filter if any of its LEDs match.

The report count at the top reads "X of Y reports" whenever a filter has narrowed things down, showing both how many match and how many exist in total for that view; it just shows the total when nothing's filtered.

See My Reports & Folders and Bulk Actions — Categorize & Delete for other ways to work with a filtered list.

title: Bulk Actions — Categorize & Delete
content:
Once you've checked one or more reports on My Reports, three buttons appear: Compare, Categorize, and Delete.

Categorize opens a modal with all six category types (Light Brand, Light Model, LED CCT, LED Brand, LED Model, Optic), each searchable, so you can tag several reports at once instead of one at a time. The "Overwrite Existing Values" checkbox controls what happens to reports that already have a value in a category you're setting:
• Checked — every selected report gets the values you chose, replacing whatever was there before.
• Unchecked — only reports with no existing value in that category are updated; reports that already have one are left alone.

LED Brand, LED Model and LED CCT are set as single values here, which suits lights with one LED. A light with several LEDs keeps each LED's brand, model and CCT together, so for those use the report's own LED cards (see LED Details — Brand, LED & CCT).

Delete permanently removes the selected reports after a confirmation showing exactly how many will be deleted. This can't be undone. Delete and Categorize are only available on My Reports — you can't delete or categorize reports from the Explore tab.

See Filtering & Search for narrowing down which reports you're selecting from.

title: LED Details — Brand, LED & CCT
content:
Tell hCRI.io which LED(s) a light uses so the report can be found, filtered and compared.

ONE OR SEVERAL LEDS
A light can have more than one kind of LED (for example a warm Nichia 519A plus a red Luminus SST-20-DR, or two CCTs of the same emitter). Each LED has its own brand, LED (model) and CCT, and they stay together, so the pairing is never mixed up. A deep-red LED simply has no CCT.

SETTING THEM
• On a report, open the editor (Source details) and use the LED cards: pick or type the brand, LED and CCT, press "Add LED" for another, and "Remove" to drop one. Removing every LED clears them.
• In Quick Fill, accepting a suggestion sets the LED from the closest matching reports.
• From the hCRI Companion app, the LED window works the same way and the LEDs go up with the report. Through the API, send a list of {brand, led, cct} (see Uploading via the API).

VALUES NOT IN THE LISTS
The brand, LED and CCT lists are curated. Choosing a value that isn't in a list sends it for admin review and leaves that field blank until it's approved (admins add values directly). Lumens and current are free numbers.

SEEN WITH
In an LED card, models that other reports have used with the brand you chose are listed first under "Seen with <brand>". It's a convenience built from how people have tagged reports, not a fixed catalogue: you can still pick any model from the full list.

WHERE THEY SHOW
Each LED is listed on the TM-30 report (LED and CCT lines, one per LED), in the report's details, and in the Explore and My Reports filters. A report matches an LED filter if any of its LEDs match.

See Filtering & Search and Bulk Actions — Categorize & Delete for working with many reports at once.

title: Calculation Methods & Sources
content:
hCRI.io implements the following standards:

CCT — Robertson's method (1968), "Computation of Correlated Color Temperature and Distribution Temperature," JOSA 58(11).

Duv — Standard CIE u'v' chromaticity arithmetic per CIE 224:2017.

CRI Ra / R1–R15 — CIE 13.3-1995. TCS reflectances, Von Kries chromatic adaptation, CIE 1964 U*V*W* color space.

TM-30 Rf and Rg — ANSI/IES TM-30-18:
• 99 CES spectral reflectances
• CIE 1964 10-degree CMFs
• CIECAM02 appearance model (CIE 159:2004)
• CAM02-UCS uniform color space (Luo, Cui & Li, 2006)
• Rf from mean ΔE in Jp,ap,bp space
• Rg from polygon area ratio of 16 hue-bin averages

Reference Illuminant — Planckian below 4000K, CIE Daylight above 5000K, linear blend between — per TM-30-18 §4.2.

MacAdam Ellipses — standard 25-ellipse dataset (MacAdam 1942), displayed at 5× and 10× scale.

Chromaticity spaces — CIE 1931 xy, CIE 1960 uv, CIE 1976 u'v'. Spectral locus computed from CIE 1931 2° CMFs.

SPD interpolation — linear to 5nm grid per TM-30 and CIE 224.

See The Technology Behind hCRI.io for the broader stack this calculation engine runs on.

title: Uploading via the API
content:
You can upload reports programmatically instead of using this website. Create a personal API token in Profile → API, then POST a file to the upload endpoint.

ENDPOINT
POST https://www.hcri.io/index.php/api/v1/upload

AUTHENTICATION
Send your token in the Authorization header:
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN

Tokens never expire. Create or revoke them anytime in Profile → API. Treat a token like a password.

SENDING A FILE
Use multipart/form-data with a "file" field, plus an optional "label". To overwrite one of your own reports instead of creating a new one (for example when re-uploading a reading), add "replaceId" with that report's id; it keeps the report's id, link, visibility, notes and LEDs. Accepted formats match the site: CSV, TSV, TXT, JSON, SP, and PDF, up to 10 MB.

EXAMPLE (curl)
curl -X POST "https://www.hcri.io/index.php/api/v1/upload" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@measurement.csv" \
  -F "label=My Light"

RESPONSE
A successful upload returns HTTP 201 (200 with "replaced": true when replaceId updated an existing report) with the report's metrics as JSON (id, cct, duv, x, y, Rf, Rg, ra, r9, and more). New uploads follow your Profile → Privacy default for Explore visibility.

ERRORS
• 401 — missing or invalid token
• 400 — no file provided
• 413 — file larger than 10 MB
• 405 — wrong HTTP method
• 422 — the file could not be parsed

QUICK TEST
A browser tester is available at /api-test.html — paste a token, choose a file, and see the response.

FLICKER READINGS
Flicker readings (from the hCRI Companion app) use the same token. POST JSON to https://www.hcri.io/index.php/api/v1/flicker with frequencyHz, percentFlicker, flickerIndex, cycleMs, waveform (array of samples) and optionally label, notes, model, spanMs, capturedAt, settings and reportId (attaches it to one of your reports). A successful call returns 201 with {success, id, reportId}. See Flicker Readings.

LED DETAILS AND SHARE LINKS
The same token can read the LED lists (GET /api/v1/led_lists), ask for an LED suggestion for a spectrum (POST /api/v1/led_suggest) and get a link to a report (POST /api/v1/reports/{id}/share).

To set a report's LEDs, POST /api/v1/reports/{id}/led with a list of LEDs, each with brand, led and cct, so a light with two LEDs keeps each one's brand, model and CCT together. An empty list removes all of them. The same call also accepts light_brand, light_model, optic, lumens, current and notes.

FULL REFERENCE
Download the API reference (PDF) from Profile → API, or at https://www.hcri.io/assets/hcri-api-spec.pdf.

See Profile & Account Settings for managing your API tokens, and What files can I upload? for the accepted formats.

title: Flicker Readings
content:
Flicker readings measure how fast (Hz) and how deeply (%) a light pulses, along with the flicker index, cycle time and the captured waveform. They come from the hCRI Companion app with meters that support flicker.

WHERE THEY SHOW UP
• Explore → Flicker lists your flicker readings. Select two or more and Compare to overlay them.
• Open a reading to see its waveform, numbers and risk tip, and to edit its title and notes or attach it to a report.
• A report's Flicker section (near the bottom) lists every flicker reading attached to it. A report can have many; a reading belongs to at most one report.

HOW THEY GET HERE
• With a reading: when the app uploads a reading that has a flicker sample, the flicker is attached to the new report automatically.
• On their own: the app's Flicker tab can upload a stand-alone sample with a title and notes. It appears under Explore → Flicker until you attach it to a report.

Deleting a report keeps its flicker readings and detaches them. Delete a flicker reading from its page. To upload from your own scripts, see Uploading via the API.

title: Runtime Curves
content:
Runtime curves show how a light's output changes over time (for example brightness stepping down as a flashlight heats up). They are private to you.

EXPLORE → RUNTIME
• The list groups your lights, each with a sparkline and retention at 1, 5, 10 and 30 minutes.
• Click a light for its own chart. Its page is ?explore=runtime&rt=<id>, so Back and Refresh keep you there.
• Tick two or more lights and press Compare to overlay them. The comparison has its own address (?explore=runtime&cmp=<ids>), so refreshing the browser keeps the same comparison, and Back returns to the list.
• Share comparison link makes a public link to the overlay and shows it as copying, then "Link copied" with a short confirmation.

UPLOADING
Upload a CSV whose first column is minutes and which has one column per light. Admins choose which user to upload for from a dropdown with type-ahead. A .json file adds meter readings (CCT, Duv, CRI, R9, Rf, Rg) to lights you already have.

ADMINS
The "working on" dropdown lists only users who have runtimes, and a refresh keeps the selected user.

See Comparing Reports for comparing reports and Flicker Readings for flicker.

title: The Technology Behind hCRI.io
content:
hCRI.io is built with a deliberately lean stack — no heavy frontend framework tooling beyond what's needed, and no backend framework at all.

FRONTEND
• React 19, built with Vite
• Three.js for the 3D CRI playground
• Canvas-based rendering for charts (SPD, CVG, CRI bars, chromaticity diagrams) rather than an external charting library
• Hand-rolled styling — no CSS framework; dark/light theme via a React context

BACKEND
• PHP, no framework — a single entry point handles routing
• PDO/MySQL for the database
• FPDF for generating downloadable TM-30 PDF reports
• PHPMailer for outgoing email (password resets, contact form)
• Apache with mod_rewrite for URL routing in production

OTHER
• Umami for cookieless, privacy-respecting analytics
• Argyll CMS .sp format support alongside CSV/TSV/JSON spectral data ingestion

For the color-science implementation specifically, see Calculation Methods & Sources.
